_note: PI Coach independent evaluation framework. Authored from general, public-domain business and marketing concepts (the material in any introductory business curriculum), in our own words, structure, grouping, and id scheme. It is NOT DECA/MBA Research's performance-indicator list: no PI text, codes, groupings, or event-to-PI mapping appears here or was reproduced. DECA's PI catalog was consulted ONLY to confirm we cover the same broad topic territory at a realistic density (so the practice feels like a real role-play), never as wording to copy or paraphrase. Structure is two-level: 13 domains, each split into our own topics, each holding several indicators. Each indicator is grain-sized so a student can explain it inside a role-play's time. `definition` is a coaching question; `strong_looks_like`/`weak_looks_like` are the honest quality bar the grader uses so scoring is not keyword-inflated. See framework-notes.md.

domains.name: Business Law
domains.blurb: Recognizing the legal dimension of business decisions: contracts, liability, regulation, ownership, and protecting what the business owns.

domains.name: Communication
domains.blurb: Making ideas land: clear structure, the right message for the audience, sound persuasion, listening, writing, and negotiation.

domains.name: Customer Relations
domains.blurb: Winning, serving, keeping, and repairing relationships with the people a business serves.

domains.name: Economics
domains.blurb: Reasoning about markets, competition, scarcity, money, and the outside forces that shape what a business can do.

domains.name: Emotional Intelligence
domains.blurb: Reading yourself and others, acting with integrity, and leading people through the human side of business.

domains.name: Entrepreneurship
domains.blurb: Spotting opportunity, shaping a business model, taking smart risks, planning, and building something that can grow.

domains.name: Financial Analysis
domains.blurb: Where money comes from and goes: cost, profit, price, budgets, statements, investment, and backing claims with numbers.

domains.name: Human Resources
domains.blurb: Finding, growing, motivating, holding accountable, and retaining the people who do the work.

domains.name: Marketing
domains.blurb: Choosing who to serve and how: target market, research, the offer, its price, place, promotion, selling, brand, and metrics.

domains.name: Information Management
domains.blurb: Turning data and research into decisions, and handling information and technology responsibly.

domains.name: Operations
domains.blurb: Getting the work done reliably: process, quality, supply, logistics, projects, safety, and operational risk.

domains.name: Professional Development
domains.blurb: Carrying yourself as a professional and taking ownership of your own growth, goals, and reputation.

domains.name: Strategic Management
domains.blurb: Weighing trade-offs, aligning to goals, reading the situation, and coordinating a coherent, measurable strategy.

criteria.name: Legal Environment Awareness
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize that laws, courts, and regulation set boundaries around a business decision, rather than reasoning as if only commercial factors applied?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Notices that a rule, permission, or legal boundary bears on the choice and keeps the plan inside it, treating the legal context as real.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes anything goes; no awareness that the situation has a legal dimension at all.
criteria.coaches: Seeing the legal boundaries around a decision

criteria.name: Forms of Business Ownership
criteria.definition: When the situation turns on how the business is structured, who owns it and who is on the hook, does the response recognize that the form of ownership carries real legal and financial consequences?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that the ownership structure affects liability, taxes, and control, and reasons about which fits the situation.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats the business form as irrelevant; ignores who bears the risk or how ownership shapes the options.
criteria.coaches: Understanding how business structure shapes risk and control

criteria.name: Contract Formation and Terms
criteria.definition: Does the response treat an agreement as something to define clearly, who owes what, on what terms, rather than leaving the deal vague or informal?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies the key terms that should be pinned down before committing and why each matters to protecting the business.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Relies on a handshake or 'we'll figure it out'; no terms, no clarity about what each side is actually agreeing to.
criteria.coaches: Defining clear terms in an agreement

criteria.name: Obligations and Remedies
criteria.definition: Does the response consider what happens if a party doesn't hold up their end, the consequence or recourse, rather than assuming everyone will simply perform?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Anticipates non-performance and builds in a consequence, safeguard, or way to make the business whole if the other side falls short.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes the deal will go perfectly; no thought to what recourse exists if it doesn't.
criteria.coaches: Planning for what happens if an agreement is broken

criteria.name: Authority to Bind the Business
criteria.definition: Does the response consider who actually has authority to make a commitment on the business's behalf, rather than assuming anyone's word binds the company?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that only certain people can commit the business and checks that a deal is made by someone with the authority to make it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes any employee or party can bind the business; commits or relies on a commitment no one was authorized to make.
criteria.coaches: Knowing who can commit the business

criteria.name: Consumer Protection and Fair Dealing
criteria.definition: Does the response respect the rules that protect customers, honest claims, product safety, fair terms, rather than treating customers as fair game to mislead?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Keeps claims honest and terms fair, and recognizes a duty not to deceive or endanger customers.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Proposes a misleading claim, hidden term, or unsafe shortcut; treats customer protection as irrelevant.
criteria.coaches: Dealing with customers honestly and lawfully

criteria.name: Regulatory Compliance and Permissions
criteria.definition: Does the response account for the licenses, standards, or industry rules the business must satisfy, rather than assuming it can operate without them?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes a permit, standard, or regulation that applies and builds compliance into the plan.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores an obvious licensing or regulatory requirement; treats compliance as optional red tape.
criteria.coaches: Operating within licensing and regulatory requirements

criteria.name: Warranties and Product Responsibility
criteria.definition: When the business stands behind a product or service, does the response treat that promise as a real obligation, honoring it and managing the exposure, rather than ignoring what the business owes buyers after the sale?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes the promise made to buyers (a warranty or guarantee) as binding, and manages both honoring it and limiting undue exposure.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores post-sale obligations; makes a promise the business can't honor, or refuses one it clearly owes.
criteria.coaches: Standing behind what the business sells

criteria.name: Employment and Workplace Law Basics
criteria.definition: Does the response handle people-decisions within legal limits, fair treatment, non-discrimination, safe conditions, rather than as if the employer could act with no constraints?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that hiring, firing, or workplace decisions carry legal limits and keeps the action fair and lawful.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Proposes an action that would be discriminatory, unsafe, or otherwise unlawful; no awareness of employee protections.

criteria.name: Intellectual Property Protection
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize when a name, design, invention, or creative work is worth protecting, and how to protect it, rather than leaving a distinctive asset exposed?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names a specific asset worth guarding and a concrete way to protect it, tying that protection to a business advantage.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Gives away or exposes something valuable; assumes anyone could copy it with no consequence.

criteria.name: Privacy and Data Obligations
criteria.definition: Does the response treat the personal data the business holds as something it has a legal duty to protect and use appropriately, rather than as free to collect and use however it likes?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes a legal duty around how personal information is collected, used, and protected, and keeps the plan within it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Collects or uses customer data with no regard to consent or protection; treats personal data as unrestricted.
criteria.coaches: Handling personal data within legal limits

criteria.name: Business Liability Awareness
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize where the business could be held responsible for harm, to customers, employees, or others, and act to limit that exposure?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Spots a realistic way the business could be held liable and takes a concrete step to reduce or manage that exposure.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores a clear liability risk; assumes nothing could go wrong or that the business would never be held responsible.

criteria.name: Resolving Disputes
criteria.definition: When a legal disagreement arises, does the response weigh how best to resolve it: negotiation, mediation, or formal action, rather than defaulting to a fight or caving entirely?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Weighs the cost and benefit of different ways to resolve a dispute and chooses one that protects the business's interests proportionately.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Jumps straight to a lawsuit or simply gives in; no thought to a proportionate way to resolve the disagreement.
criteria.coaches: Choosing a sensible way to resolve a dispute

criteria.name: Ethical Governance and Compliance Culture
criteria.definition: Does the response support a culture where rules and ethics are actually followed, clear standards, accountability, rather than treating compliance as something to work around?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Builds compliance and ethical conduct into how the business operates, with clear standards and accountability, not just lip service.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats rules as obstacles to dodge; tolerates a wink-and-nod culture; no mechanism to keep conduct honest.
criteria.coaches: Building a culture of compliance and ethics

criteria.name: Clear and Organized Ideas
criteria.definition: Is the response organized so a listener can follow it, a clear main point and ideas in a sensible order, rather than a pile of loosely related statements?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Opens with the point, moves through it in a logical order, and each part builds on the last; the listener always knows where they are.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Jumps between ideas, buries the main point, or lists tactics with no thread the listener can follow.
criteria.coaches: Organizing a message so it is easy to follow

criteria.name: Concise and Precise Expression
criteria.definition: Does the response say what it means efficiently and exactly, rather than padding, rambling, or hiding the point behind vague words?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Makes each point in clear, specific language and stops; no filler, no vagueness where a precise word was available.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Rambling or repetitive; vague generalities where specifics were needed; the listener has to dig for the actual meaning.

criteria.name: Explaining Complex Ideas Simply
criteria.definition: When something is technical or complicated, does the response make it understandable to the listener, rather than losing them in jargon or detail?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Translates a complex idea into plain terms, uses an example or analogy, and checks that it lands for this audience.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Buries the point in jargon or detail; assumes the listener already understands; no attempt to make it accessible.
criteria.coaches: Making complex ideas easy to understand

criteria.name: Explaining the Reasoning
criteria.definition: Does the response explain WHY, not just WHAT, giving the reasoning behind a recommendation so the listener can trust it, rather than issuing a conclusion with no rationale?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Walks the listener through the reasoning so they understand not just the recommendation but why it follows.
criteria.weak_looks_like: States what to do with no why; expects the listener to accept a conclusion on assertion alone.
criteria.coaches: Showing the reasoning behind a recommendation

criteria.name: Audience Adaptation
criteria.definition: Does the response speak to the specific person in the room: their role, priorities, and what they care about, rather than delivering a generic pitch that would fit anyone?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Frames the message around what this particular audience values and adjusts emphasis accordingly.
criteria.weak_looks_like: One-size-fits-all delivery; leads with details the audience wouldn't care about and omits what they would.
criteria.coaches: Tailoring a message to the specific audience

criteria.name: Professional Tone and Register
criteria.definition: Is the message pitched with the right level of formality and credibility for a business setting, rather than too casual, defensive, or overhyped for the stakes?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reads as poised and credible; confident without overclaiming, respectful even under challenge.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Too casual for the stakes, gets defensive, or overhypes; misjudges the register the situation calls for.
criteria.coaches: Matching tone to a professional setting

criteria.name: Choosing the Right Channel
criteria.definition: Does the response pick the appropriate medium for the message, a conversation, an email, a formal document, rather than defaulting to whatever is easiest regardless of fit?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Chooses the communication channel that fits the message and audience (sensitive news in person, a record in writing).
criteria.weak_looks_like: Uses the wrong medium for the stakes; a sensitive matter handled carelessly, or a simple note made needlessly formal.
criteria.coaches: Choosing the right medium for a message

criteria.name: Persuasive Reasoning
criteria.definition: Does the response give the listener actual reasons to agree, evidence, benefits, a logical case, rather than just asserting that the idea is good?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Backs the recommendation with reasons and evidence, connects it to what the audience gains, and anticipates the obvious objection.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Asserts a conclusion as self-evident; 'this will work' with no support; relies on enthusiasm instead of a case.

criteria.name: Framing and Emphasis
criteria.definition: Does the response frame the message to land, leading with what matters most, framing the choice in the listener's terms, rather than presenting everything flatly?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Leads with the strongest point, frames the decision around a benefit or stakes the listener feels, and makes the takeaway memorable.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Presents everything at equal weight; buries the strongest argument; no framing that helps the point stick.
criteria.coaches: Framing a message so the key point lands

criteria.name: Using Examples and Stories
criteria.definition: Does the response make a point concrete with an example, story, or illustration, rather than staying abstract and forgettable?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Uses a well-chosen example or short story to make an abstract point vivid and memorable for this audience.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Stays entirely abstract; no illustration; the point is technically stated but nothing helps it stick.
criteria.coaches: Making a point concrete with an example

criteria.name: Negotiation Communication
criteria.definition: When interests differ, does the response bargain toward an agreement both sides can accept, trading, finding common ground, rather than demanding or immediately conceding?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Seeks a workable agreement by understanding the other side's interests and trading toward mutual gain, not just winning.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Makes demands with no give, or caves at the first push; treats negotiation as a battle to win or a loss to accept.

criteria.name: Active Listening
criteria.definition: Does the response show it actually heard what was said, reflecting the real concern back, rather than talking past the other person?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Restates or acknowledges the other side's actual point before responding, showing it registered what they meant.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores what was said; responds to a version of the question that wasn't asked; talks over the concern.
criteria.coaches: Genuinely hearing what the other person said

criteria.name: Asking Effective Questions
criteria.definition: Does the response ask the questions that surface what it needs to know, about the situation, the customer, the constraints, rather than proceeding on assumptions?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Asks a pointed question that would genuinely change the plan, aimed at the real unknown rather than a formality.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Asks nothing and assumes; or asks vague questions that wouldn't actually inform the decision.
criteria.coaches: Asking questions that surface what matters

criteria.name: Reading the Other Person's Signals
criteria.definition: Does the response pick up on the other party's reactions and cues (hesitation, interest, confusion) and adjust, rather than plowing ahead regardless?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Notices how the other person is reacting and adjusts the approach: slows down, clarifies, or shifts tack accordingly.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Presses on deaf to the other person's cues; misses obvious signs of confusion, resistance, or interest.
criteria.coaches: Reading and responding to the other party's cues

criteria.name: Handling Objections and Tough Questions
criteria.definition: When challenged, does the response engage the specific objection with a real answer, rather than restating the pitch, dodging, or getting defensive?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Directly addresses the objection, acknowledges the concern behind it, and defends or adjusts the position with a reason.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Deflects, repeats earlier points, or gets defensive; the actual concern goes unanswered.

criteria.name: Written Communication
criteria.definition: When the situation calls for something written, an email, notice, or report, does the response make it clear, correct, and appropriate for the reader?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Structures the written message for the reader, states purpose and next step clearly, and matches tone to the situation.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Rambling, unclear, or inappropriate in tone; no clear purpose or ask; leaves the reader unsure what to do.
criteria.coaches: Writing clearly for a business reader

criteria.name: Giving and Receiving Feedback
criteria.definition: Does the response handle feedback constructively, giving it specifically and kindly, or taking it without defensiveness, rather than avoiding it or reacting badly?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Gives feedback that is specific and actionable, or receives criticism openly and uses it; treats feedback as useful.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Gives vague or harsh feedback; or reacts to criticism defensively; treats feedback as an attack.

criteria.name: Communicating Difficult Messages
criteria.definition: When the news is hard, a rejection, a problem, a no, does the response deliver it honestly and with care, rather than dodging, sugarcoating, or being needlessly blunt?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Delivers the hard message clearly and honestly while showing respect for the other person and offering a path forward.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Avoids or buries the bad news, misleads to soften it, or delivers it callously with no regard for the recipient.
criteria.coaches: Delivering hard news honestly and with care

criteria.name: Facilitating a Discussion
criteria.definition: When more than two people are involved, does the response help the group communicate, drawing people out, keeping it on track, rather than dominating or letting it drift?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Guides a group toward a productive outcome, inviting input and keeping the conversation focused.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Dominates the discussion or lets it wander; some voices are ignored; the group reaches no clear outcome.

criteria.name: Following Up and Confirming Understanding
criteria.definition: Does the response close the loop, confirming what was agreed and following up, rather than assuming a message was received and understood?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Confirms mutual understanding and follows up on commitments, so nothing important is left to assumption.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes the message landed and the task will happen; no confirmation, no follow-up; loose ends left dangling.

criteria.name: Understanding Customer Needs
criteria.definition: Does the response start from what the customer actually wants or struggles with, discovered, not assumed, rather than pushing a solution the business happens to prefer?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies the real underlying need or frustration, distinguishes what different customers want, and shapes the response around it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes what customers want; talks about the product without ever naming a customer need; treats all customers as identical.
criteria.coaches: Discovering and centering the customer's real needs

criteria.name: Personalizing the Experience
criteria.definition: Does the response use what's known about a customer to make them feel individually served, rather than treating everyone with the same generic script?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Uses customer history or context to tailor the interaction so the customer feels recognized and understood.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Identical treatment for everyone; ignores what's known about the customer; a generic script where personalization was possible.
criteria.coaches: Personalizing service using what you know

criteria.name: Setting Customer Expectations
criteria.definition: Does the response set honest, clear expectations up front, what the customer will and won't get, rather than overpromising and disappointing later?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Sets accurate expectations about what will happen and when, so the customer isn't surprised or let down.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Overpromises to win the moment; leaves expectations vague; sets the customer up to be disappointed.

criteria.name: Delivering Service Quality
criteria.definition: Does the response commit to a standard of service the customer can rely on, responsiveness, care, following through, rather than a vague promise of being 'good'?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Defines what good service concretely means here and how it will be delivered consistently, not just asserted.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Vague 'we'll give great service' with no mechanism; no standard the customer could actually count on.

criteria.name: Managing Difficult Interactions
criteria.definition: When a customer is upset or unreasonable, does the response stay professional and steer toward resolution, rather than matching their emotion or giving up?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Stays calm, de-escalates, and keeps the interaction moving toward a workable outcome without losing composure.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Gets defensive or matches the customer's heat; caves entirely; lets the interaction spiral with no path to resolution.

criteria.name: Serving Diverse Customers
criteria.definition: Does the response adapt to customers with different needs, backgrounds, or abilities, rather than assuming one approach serves everyone equally?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that customers differ and adapts service so a range of customers feel well served and included.
criteria.weak_looks_like: One approach for all; overlooks accessibility or difference; alienates customers who don't fit the default.

criteria.name: Customer Relationship Thinking
criteria.definition: Does the response show how the business will identify, keep, and deepen customer relationships over time, rather than treating customers as one-time transactions?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Uses customer data or loyalty to make customers feel known; distinguishes new versus returning customers; ties retention to a specific mechanism.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats customers as one-time sales; vague 'good service' with no mechanism; no retention thinking at all.
criteria.coaches: Building and sustaining customer relationships over time

criteria.name: Building Rapport and Trust
criteria.definition: Does the response work to earn the customer's trust, honesty, reliability, standing behind the product, rather than optimizing a single sale at the relationship's expense?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Chooses actions that build credibility (honesty about limits, standing behind quality) and connects trust to future business.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Prioritizes a short-term win in a way that would erode trust; overpromises to close; treats trust as irrelevant.

criteria.name: Customer Lifetime Value
criteria.definition: Does the response weigh what a customer is worth over the whole relationship, not just this one sale, when deciding how much to invest in keeping them happy?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reasons about the long-run value of a customer and justifies investing in the relationship because of the repeat business it protects.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Judges the customer only by the current transaction; won't invest to keep them because it can't see beyond one sale.
criteria.coaches: Valuing customers over the whole relationship

criteria.name: Building Loyalty and Repeat Business
criteria.definition: Does the response give customers a concrete reason to come back, rather than assuming a satisfied customer will automatically return?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names a specific mechanism (a loyalty structure, follow-up, or reason to return) tied to why customers would choose the business again.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes satisfaction alone drives repeat business; no mechanism; treats every sale as a fresh start.

criteria.name: Turning Customers into Advocates
criteria.definition: Does the response turn happy customers into a source of new business, referrals, reviews, word-of-mouth, rather than leaving their goodwill untapped?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Creates a concrete reason and easy way for satisfied customers to refer others or spread the word.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Leaves goodwill on the table; no mechanism to turn a happy customer into referrals or reviews.

criteria.name: Handling Complaints and Service Recovery
criteria.definition: When a customer is unhappy, does the response resolve the problem and rebuild the relationship, not just end the interaction, turning a bad moment into retained trust?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Acknowledges the experience, offers a concrete fix, and addresses why it happened so it won't recur; aims to keep the customer.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Defensive, dismissive, or purely transactional; no attempt to repair the relationship or prevent a repeat.
criteria.coaches: Resolving problems in a way that keeps the customer

criteria.name: Winning Back At-Risk Customers
criteria.definition: When a customer is about to leave or has left, does the response try to win them back with a genuine fix, rather than writing them off?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes an at-risk or lost customer as worth recovering and makes a real, targeted effort to bring them back.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Writes off a leaving customer; no attempt to understand why or to win them back; treats churn as inevitable.
criteria.coaches: Recovering customers at risk of leaving

criteria.name: Gathering Customer Feedback
criteria.definition: Does the response seek out what customers actually think, asking, listening, learning from it, rather than assuming it already knows how they feel?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Sets up a concrete way to hear from customers and uses what they say to improve, treating feedback as a signal.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes it knows what customers think; no channel to hear from them; ignores or dismisses the feedback it does get.
criteria.coaches: Actively gathering and using customer feedback

criteria.name: Reputation and Word-of-Mouth
criteria.definition: Does the response consider how an interaction affects the business's wider reputation, reviews, referrals, what customers tell others, rather than treating it as isolated?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that how this customer is treated ripples into reputation and referrals, and factors that into the choice.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats the interaction as private and consequence-free; ignores reviews, referrals, and reputation entirely.

criteria.name: Following Up After the Sale
criteria.definition: Does the response care for the customer after the purchase, checking in, ensuring satisfaction, rather than treating the sale as the end of the relationship?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Plans concrete post-sale follow-up that confirms satisfaction and opens the door to future business.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Disappears once the sale closes; no follow-up; the customer is on their own after paying.
criteria.coaches: Caring for the customer after the sale

criteria.name: Scarcity and Trade-offs
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize that resources are limited and that choosing one thing means giving up another, weighing what's forgone, rather than treating options as free?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names what is given up by a choice (the opportunity cost) and justifies why this use of limited resources beats the alternative.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Proposes doing everything with no acknowledgment of limits; treats time, money, or attention as unlimited.
criteria.coaches: Weighing opportunity cost under limited resources

criteria.name: Value and Economic Utility
criteria.definition: Does the response reason about what makes something valuable to a customer, form, availability, timing, ease, rather than assuming value is fixed or obvious?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies a specific way the business creates value for the customer (better form, place, time, or ease of getting it).
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes the product is valuable just because it exists; no account of what actually makes it worth paying for.
criteria.coaches: Understanding what creates value for customers

criteria.name: Profit Motive and Risk-Reward
criteria.definition: Does the response understand that businesses take on risk in pursuit of profit, and weigh the reward against the risk, rather than treating profit as guaranteed or risk as free?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Weighs the potential reward of a move against the risk taken to earn it, treating profit as the payoff for bearing risk.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes profit is automatic; takes risk with no eye on the reward, or expects reward with no risk.
criteria.coaches: Weighing reward against the risk taken to earn it

criteria.name: Productivity and Specialization
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize that dividing work and using resources efficiently produces more with less, rather than ignoring how output per effort could be raised?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reasons about getting more output from the same resources through specialization, better tools, or smarter division of work.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores productivity; assumes output only grows by adding more people or hours regardless of efficiency.
criteria.coaches: Raising output per unit of effort

criteria.name: Supply and Demand
criteria.definition: Does the response reason about how much customers want something versus how available it is, and what that means for price and sales?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Connects a pricing or output choice to demand and availability, and anticipates how a shift would change customer behavior.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Sets price or volume with no reference to demand or supply; assumes customers will buy any amount at any price.

criteria.name: Price Sensitivity
criteria.definition: Does the response consider how customers would react to a price change, some hardly flinch, others walk away, rather than assuming demand is unaffected by price?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Judges how sensitive these customers are to price and uses that to inform how far price can move.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes a price change has no effect on demand, or that lowering price always raises total revenue.
criteria.coaches: Judging how customers respond to price

criteria.name: Incentives and Behavior
criteria.definition: Does the response consider how the incentives it sets up will shape behavior, customers, employees, partners responding to rewards and costs, rather than assuming people act as told?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Anticipates how the incentives created will actually drive behavior, including unintended responses.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes people will behave as intended regardless of the incentives; ignores how rewards and costs shape action.

criteria.name: Market Structure and Competition
criteria.definition: Does the response account for how competitive the market is (many rivals, few, or none) and what that means for the business's freedom to act?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reads the competitive intensity of the market and adjusts expectations about pricing power and differentiation accordingly.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores how crowded or contested the market is; assumes the business can act as if it had no competition.
criteria.coaches: Reading the competitiveness of a market

criteria.name: Business Risk and Uncertainty
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize the different ways a business venture can fail (market, economic, competitive) and account for that uncertainty, rather than treating the future as known?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies the real sources of uncertainty in the situation and factors them into the plan instead of assuming a single outcome.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats the future as certain; plans for one scenario only; ignores the ways things could turn out differently.
criteria.coaches: Accounting for business risk and uncertainty

criteria.name: Economic Conditions and Cycles
criteria.definition: Does the response account for the broader economy, growth or downturn, rising costs, employment, that shapes what's realistic right now?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reads the current economic climate (a downturn, inflation, a boom) and adapts the plan to fit it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes conditions are static and favorable; a plan that only works in an ideal economy.
criteria.coaches: Adapting to the broader economic climate

criteria.name: Cost of Doing Business
criteria.definition: Does the response account for the real costs of producing and operating, labor, materials, productivity, rather than treating output as costless?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes what it costs to produce or deliver and how productivity affects that, and factors it into the decision.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores production and operating costs; assumes more output is always better regardless of what it costs to make.
criteria.coaches: Accounting for the real cost of producing

criteria.name: Reading Economic Indicators
criteria.definition: When broad signals matter, inflation, employment, growth, interest rates, does the response read them and draw the right implication, rather than ignoring them?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Interprets a relevant economic indicator correctly and draws a sensible implication for the business's decision.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores economic signals that clearly bear on the situation, or misreads what they imply.
criteria.coaches: Reading economic signals and their implications

criteria.name: Money, Credit, and Interest
criteria.definition: Does the response reason about the role of money and credit, that borrowing has a cost and timing matters, rather than treating financing as free or instant?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that credit carries a cost and that the timing and terms of money matter to the decision.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats borrowing as costless; ignores interest or terms; assumes money is always available when needed.
criteria.coaches: Understanding the cost and role of credit

criteria.name: Government's Role in the Economy
criteria.definition: Does the response account for how taxes, regulation, or public spending shape the business's environment, rather than reasoning as if government had no effect?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes a relevant way government action (a tax, a regulation, a program) affects the situation and factors it in.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores taxes, regulation, or public policy that clearly bear on the decision.
criteria.coaches: Accounting for government's effect on business

criteria.name: Global and Trade Forces
criteria.definition: Does the response consider forces beyond the local market, trade, global suppliers, currency, when they bear on the situation?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes a relevant external or global factor (a supply disruption, trade condition, currency shift) and accounts for it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Reasons as if the business were sealed off from wider forces that clearly affect it.
criteria.coaches: Accounting for global and trade forces

criteria.name: Spillover Effects and Externalities
criteria.definition: Does the response notice costs or benefits its decision imposes on others outside the transaction, community, environment, third parties, rather than counting only its own ledger?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes an effect the decision has on parties outside the deal and weighs it, rather than ignoring the spillover.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Counts only direct costs and benefits; ignores harm or benefit to the community, environment, or bystanders.

criteria.name: Self-Awareness
criteria.definition: Does the response show honest awareness of its own limits and blind spots, acknowledging what it doesn't know, rather than projecting false certainty?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names the limits of its own knowledge or position honestly and factors that into the decision.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Projects certainty untethered from what's actually known; no awareness of its own gaps or biases.

criteria.name: Composure Under Pressure
criteria.definition: Does the response stay steady and constructive when challenged or under stress, rather than getting rattled, defensive, or reactive?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Stays calm and problem-focused under a tough question or high stakes; separates emotion from the decision.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Gets flustered or defensive when pushed; lets pressure drive a reactive or scattered response.

criteria.name: Managing Stress and Emotions
criteria.definition: Does the response manage its own emotional response so it doesn't distort judgment, rather than letting frustration or excitement drive the decision?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Keeps emotion in check so the reasoning stays sound; doesn't let a strong feeling override good judgment.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Lets frustration, panic, or overexcitement drive the choice; emotion visibly distorts the reasoning.

criteria.name: Decisiveness
criteria.definition: Does the response actually make a call and commit to it, rather than dithering, hedging endlessly, or dodging the decision the situation demands?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Commits to a clear decision with a reason, accepting that acting is better than endless hedging once the case is clear.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Waffles or refuses to decide; hides behind 'it depends' where a decision was called for; leaves the situation unresolved.
criteria.coaches: Making a clear decision and committing

criteria.name: Personal Integrity and Ethics
criteria.definition: Does the response hold to what's right even when a cheaper or easier option exists, honesty, fairness, accountability, rather than choosing the expedient path?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes the ethical stakes, chooses the fair and honest course, and can explain why it's worth the cost.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Takes a shortcut that misleads or exploits; ignores an obvious ethical issue; frames integrity as a cost to avoid.

criteria.name: Showing Accountability
criteria.definition: When something goes wrong, does the response own its part and put it right, rather than deflecting blame or making excuses?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Takes responsibility for a mistake or outcome and focuses on fixing it, rather than assigning blame elsewhere.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Deflects, makes excuses, or blames others; won't own the part it played in the problem.
criteria.coaches: Owning mistakes and putting them right

criteria.name: Balancing Stakeholder Interests
criteria.definition: When different parties want different things, does the response weigh their interests fairly, rather than serving one at the unfair expense of the others?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes the competing interests of customers, employees, owners, and community, and seeks a fair balance among them.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Serves one party while ignoring the fair claims of others; no attempt to balance competing interests.

criteria.name: Social Responsibility
criteria.definition: Does the response weigh the business's impact on its community, employees, or environment, rather than treating profit as the only thing that matters?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Considers the wider impact of the decision and balances it against profit in a way it can justify.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores impact on community, workers, or environment; treats responsibility as irrelevant to the choice.

criteria.name: Empathy and Perspective-Taking
criteria.definition: Does the response consider how a decision lands for the other people involved, employees, customers, partners, rather than reasoning only from the business's side?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names how the decision feels or affects a specific stakeholder and adjusts to that, showing genuine understanding.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Considers only one side; treats people as obstacles or line items; no awareness of how others experience the choice.

criteria.name: Reading Social and Emotional Cues
criteria.definition: Does the response pick up on how others are feeling or reacting and respond to it, rather than pressing ahead deaf to the room?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Notices a stakeholder's likely reaction or resistance and adjusts the approach to it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores how others are reacting; presses a plan that clearly isn't landing; tone-deaf to the situation.
criteria.coaches: Reading and responding to how others feel

criteria.name: Cultural Awareness and Respect
criteria.definition: Does the response treat people of different backgrounds with respect and adjust for difference, rather than assuming everyone shares one perspective?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that customers or colleagues differ in background and needs, and adapts respectfully.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes one perspective fits all; ignores or dismisses difference; a plan that would alienate part of the audience.

criteria.name: Leadership and Direction
criteria.definition: Does the response set clear direction and take responsibility for the outcome, rather than being vague about who does what or where things are headed?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Sets a clear direction, owns the outcome, and gives people something definite to move toward.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Vague about direction or responsibility; leads by default; no one would know what to do from it.
criteria.coaches: Setting clear direction as a leader

criteria.name: Building Trust as a Leader
criteria.definition: Does the response earn the trust of the people it leads, through consistency, fairness, and following through, rather than relying on position alone?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Acts in ways that build the team's trust: consistent, fair, honest, and reliable on commitments.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Relies on authority without earning trust; inconsistent or unfair; makes commitments it doesn't keep.
criteria.coaches: Earning the trust of those you lead

criteria.name: Motivating and Inspiring Others
criteria.definition: Does the response give people a reason to care and act, purpose, recognition, buy-in, rather than assuming they'll comply just because they're told?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Gives people a reason to care and considers how to bring them along; leads through influence, not just authority.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Dictates with no buy-in; assumes compliance; no thought to morale or why anyone would follow.

criteria.name: Delegating and Empowering
criteria.definition: Does the response entrust work to others and give them room to own it, rather than hoarding every task or micromanaging?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Assigns responsibility to the right people and gives them the authority and trust to carry it out.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Tries to do everything alone or micromanages; won't trust others with real ownership.

criteria.name: Giving Recognition
criteria.definition: Does the response acknowledge and credit people's contributions, rather than taking credit or letting good work go unnoticed?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes and credits people's efforts in a way that reinforces the behavior and lifts morale.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Takes the credit or stays silent; lets good work go unacknowledged; recognition is an afterthought.

criteria.name: Mentoring and Developing Others
criteria.definition: Does the response invest in helping another person grow, guidance, encouragement, opportunity, rather than treating people as fixed tools for the task?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Takes an interest in another person's growth and offers concrete guidance or opportunity to help them develop.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats people as fixed; no interest in their growth; misses a chance to develop someone.

criteria.name: Teamwork and Collaboration
criteria.definition: Does the response work with others toward a shared goal, using their strengths, sharing credit, rather than going it alone or taking over?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Draws on others' strengths, coordinates the effort, and treats the goal as shared.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Goes it alone or steamrolls; ignores what teammates bring; treats collaboration as an obstacle.
criteria.coaches: Collaborating effectively toward a shared goal

criteria.name: Building Consensus
criteria.definition: When a group must decide, does the response bring people toward agreement they can commit to, rather than forcing a decision or leaving the group split?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Draws out concerns and finds common ground so the group reaches a decision people will actually support.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Forces a decision over objections or lets the group stay deadlocked; no buy-in behind the outcome.
criteria.coaches: Bringing a group to a decision it supports

criteria.name: Managing Team Morale
criteria.definition: Does the response attend to the group's energy and spirit, keeping people motivated through difficulty, rather than treating morale as irrelevant to performance?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Notices and tends to the team's morale, taking concrete steps to keep people motivated and engaged.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores morale; assumes people will keep performing regardless of how they feel about the work.

criteria.name: Managing Conflict
criteria.definition: When people disagree, does the response work toward a resolution that preserves the working relationship, rather than avoiding the conflict or winning at the other's expense?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Surfaces the disagreement, looks for common ground or a fair resolution, and keeps the relationship intact.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Avoids the conflict, steamrolls the other party, or lets it fester; being right matters more than the relationship.

criteria.name: Interpersonal Influence
criteria.definition: Does the response bring others around through understanding what they want, rather than pushing, pressuring, or assuming agreement?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Connects the ask to what the other person values, building genuine agreement rather than pressure.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Pushes or pressures; assumes agreement; no attempt to understand what would actually move the other person.

criteria.name: Adaptability and Openness
criteria.definition: Does the response stay open to new information and adjust, rather than rigidly defending a first position when the situation changes?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Updates its approach when new facts warrant it and treats change as something to work with, not resist.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Clings to the original stance regardless of new information; treats any change as a threat.

criteria.name: Handling Criticism Gracefully
criteria.definition: When personally criticized or challenged, does the response stay open and learn, rather than getting defensive or dismissive?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Takes criticism without defensiveness, separates the useful signal from the sting, and adjusts where warranted.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Bristles, defends, or dismisses; treats criticism as a personal attack rather than information.

criteria.name: Opportunity Recognition
criteria.definition: Does the response identify a real opportunity, an unmet need, a gap, a change worth acting on, and make the case for why it's worth pursuing now?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names a specific unmet need or opening, explains why it exists and why now, and connects it to who would pay.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Vague 'there's a market for this' with no evidence; a solution in search of a problem.

criteria.name: Validating the Idea
criteria.definition: Does the response test whether the opportunity is real before betting on it, talking to customers, running a small test, rather than assuming it will work?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Proposes a cheap, concrete way to test the key assumption before committing serious resources.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes the idea will work; skips validation; treats an untested belief as proven demand.
criteria.coaches: Testing an idea before betting on it

criteria.name: Identifying the First Customers
criteria.definition: Does the response pinpoint who would buy first and why, a specific beachhead, rather than aiming at a vague 'everyone' from day one?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names a specific early customer and why they'd buy first, giving the venture a concrete place to start.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Targets everyone at once; no idea who the first real customer is; assumes broad appeal with no starting point.

criteria.name: Value Proposition
criteria.definition: Does the response make clear what specific value the business delivers and to whom, rather than describing a product with no clear benefit or customer?
criteria.strong_looks_like: States who the customer is and the specific value they get, distinct from alternatives.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Describes features but no clear benefit or customer; a value claim that isn't distinctive.
criteria.coaches: Defining the value delivered and to whom

criteria.name: Business Model and Revenue Logic
criteria.definition: Does the response show how the business actually makes money and covers its costs, rather than an idea with no revenue logic behind it?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Explains how the business captures revenue and covers costs; the pieces fit into a model that could sustain itself.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Describes a product but not who pays or how it stays afloat; no revenue or cost logic.
criteria.coaches: Making the money side of the idea add up

criteria.name: Competitive Advantage
criteria.definition: Does the response identify what would keep the idea from being immediately copied or undercut, a real edge, rather than assuming it will stay ahead by default?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Names a durable advantage (something hard to copy) that would let the venture hold its ground against competitors.
criteria.weak_looks_like: No defensibility; anyone could copy it tomorrow; assumes a head start alone is enough to stay ahead.
criteria.coaches: Building an edge that's hard to copy

criteria.name: Resourcefulness and Bootstrapping
criteria.definition: Does the response make progress with limited resources, creative substitutes, doing more with less, rather than assuming money and staff will simply appear?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Stretches limited resources creatively and finds a way to start small rather than waiting for ideal conditions.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes resources will appear; a plan that only works with funding or staff it doesn't have.

criteria.name: Funding and Capital
criteria.definition: When the plan needs money to start or grow, does the response reason about where it comes from and its cost, rather than treating capital as free or unlimited?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Considers a realistic source of funding and its trade-offs (debt, investment, reinvested profit) for this situation.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes unlimited capital; ignores where the money comes from or what it costs to raise.
criteria.coaches: Reasoning about where funding comes from

criteria.name: Building the Founding Team
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize what skills the venture is missing and bring in the right people or partners, rather than assuming one person can do everything?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies a gap in skills or capacity and brings in the right partner, hire, or ally to fill it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes the founder can do it all; ignores missing skills; no thought to who else is needed.
criteria.coaches: Building the team the venture needs

criteria.name: Pricing a New Venture
criteria.definition: Does the response set a launch price grounded in cost, value, and the market, rather than guessing or racing to the bottom to get the first sales?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Sets an early price that reflects cost, the value delivered, and what the market will bear, and can defend it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Prices by guess or gives it away to get traction, with no path to a sustainable price later.

criteria.name: Smart Risk-Taking
criteria.definition: Does the response take risk deliberately, containing the downside while pursuing the upside, rather than avoiding all risk or betting everything blindly?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Finds a way to pursue the upside while containing the downside; risk is taken on purpose, not blindly.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Either refuses any risk or bets big with no way to limit the loss; no plan for if it fails.

criteria.name: Business Planning
criteria.definition: Does the response lay out a concrete plan to get from idea to operating business, steps, milestones, resources, rather than a vision with no path?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Sketches a realistic path from here to a working business, with concrete steps and milestones.
criteria.weak_looks_like: All vision, no plan; no steps, milestones, or sense of what happens first; skips how the idea actually gets built.
criteria.coaches: Laying out a path from idea to business

criteria.name: Growth and Scaling
criteria.definition: Does the response think about how the business grows beyond its first success, what has to change to serve more customers, rather than treating the current scale as the end state?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies what must change to grow (capacity, systems, funding) and distinguishes what works now from what scales.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes growth is automatic; a plan that only works at tiny scale; no thought to what breaks with volume.
criteria.coaches: Planning for growth beyond the first win

criteria.name: Pivoting When Needed
criteria.definition: When the evidence says the original idea isn't working, does the response change direction based on what it learned, rather than stubbornly pushing the same plan?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reads the signal that the current approach isn't working and changes direction deliberately, keeping what's learned.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Doubles down on a failing idea regardless of evidence, or abandons everything at random with no learning.
criteria.coaches: Changing direction based on what you learn

criteria.name: Resilience and Learning from Setbacks
criteria.definition: Does the response treat a setback as information to adjust from, rather than as a reason to quit or a thing to ignore?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Uses what went wrong to adjust the plan; persistent without being stubborn about a failing approach.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Gives up at the first obstacle, or ignores the setback and repeats the same mistake.

criteria.name: Long-term Vision for the Venture
criteria.definition: Does the response have a sense of where the venture is ultimately headed, what it's building toward, rather than only reacting to the next step?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Articulates where the venture is headed over time and lets that longer aim shape near-term choices.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Purely reactive; no sense of the destination; near-term moves that don't build toward anything.
criteria.coaches: Knowing where the venture is headed

criteria.name: Revenue versus Profit
criteria.definition: Does the response distinguish money coming in from money kept: recognizing that sales aren't profit until costs are covered?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Clearly separates revenue from profit and reasons about what's left after costs.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats sales as if they were profit; celebrates revenue while ignoring the costs behind it.

criteria.name: Cost Structure
criteria.definition: Does the response understand the costs behind an offer, what's fixed versus what rises with volume, rather than treating all costs as one lump or ignoring them?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Separates fixed from variable costs and uses that to reason about how profit changes with volume.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Lumps all costs together or ignores them; no sense of how costs behave as the business scales.

criteria.name: Break-even Thinking
criteria.definition: Does the response reason about the point where the business covers its costs, how much it must sell to stop losing money, rather than ignoring that threshold?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reasons about how much must be sold to cover costs and uses that to judge whether the plan is viable.
criteria.weak_looks_like: No sense of the point where costs are covered; assumes profitability without asking what volume it requires.

criteria.name: Margins and Markup
criteria.definition: Does the response reason about the profit built into each sale, the margin, rather than pricing or discounting with no idea what's left per unit?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reasons about the margin on each sale and how a price or discount affects what's left.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Discounts or prices with no idea what margin remains; assumes volume always makes up for a thin margin.
criteria.coaches: Reasoning about margin on each sale

criteria.name: Cost Control
criteria.definition: Does the response look for where costs can be reduced without harming what matters, rather than accepting every cost as fixed or cutting blindly?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies a specific cost that can be trimmed without damaging quality or value, and justifies the cut.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores cost control, or slashes costs in a way that would damage quality, service, or long-term value.

criteria.name: Pricing for Profit
criteria.definition: Does the response set or defend a price that both covers costs and reflects value, rather than pricing arbitrarily, only to undercut, or with no link to cost?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Ties price to both cost and perceived value, and can justify the number against margin and competition.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Picks a price with no reasoning; defaults to 'lower is better'; a price that wouldn't cover delivery.
criteria.coaches: Setting a price that covers cost and captures value

criteria.name: Budgeting and Resource Allocation
criteria.definition: Does the response direct limited money toward what matters most and stay within what the business can afford, rather than proposing spending with no budget in mind?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Prioritizes spending toward the highest-return use, stays inside a realistic limit, and can say what it would cut.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Proposes spending with no ceiling; funds everything equally; no sense of what the business can afford.
criteria.coaches: Allocating a limited budget to what matters

criteria.name: Cash Flow Awareness
criteria.definition: Does the response account for the timing of money in and out, not just whether it's profitable eventually, but whether it can pay its bills along the way?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that timing of cash matters, not just eventual profit, and plans for the gap between spending and earning.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes profitable means solvent; ignores the timing of cash and the risk of running out mid-plan.
criteria.coaches: Managing the timing of cash in and out

criteria.name: Managing Working Capital
criteria.definition: Does the response keep enough on hand to run day to day, covering stock, receivables, and bills, rather than tying up or draining cash the operation needs?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes the need to keep the business liquid enough to operate, balancing stock, credit given, and bills due.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ties up all the cash or ignores day-to-day liquidity; a plan that could leave the business unable to pay its bills.
criteria.coaches: Keeping enough cash to run day to day

criteria.name: Understanding the Income Statement
criteria.definition: When profit and loss are at issue, does the response reason correctly about revenue, costs, and the profit left over, rather than confusing or ignoring how they relate?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reasons soundly about how revenue minus costs yields profit, and what a change to one does to the bottom line.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Confuses revenue, cost, and profit; can't trace how a change flows to the bottom line.
criteria.coaches: Reading how revenue and costs make profit

criteria.name: Understanding What the Business Owns and Owes
criteria.definition: Does the response account for what the business owns and what it owes, its assets and obligations, rather than looking only at the flow of sales?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Considers the business's assets and debts, not just its sales, when judging its financial position.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Looks only at revenue; ignores debt or what the business owns; misjudges its financial health.
criteria.coaches: Weighing what the business owns against what it owes

criteria.name: Reading Financial Information
criteria.definition: When given numbers, a statement, a report, figures, does the response actually interpret them to inform the decision, rather than ignoring or misreading them?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Pulls the meaningful signal from the numbers provided and lets it shape the recommendation.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores the financial information given, or misreads what it says; decides as if the numbers weren't there.

criteria.name: Financial Ratios and Health
criteria.definition: Does the response use simple comparisons, profit against sales, debt against assets, to judge financial health, rather than reading raw numbers with no context?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Puts a number in context by comparing it (to sales, to last period, to a benchmark) to judge whether it's healthy.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Reads a raw figure with no comparison; can't tell whether a number is good or bad because nothing frames it.
criteria.coaches: Comparing numbers to judge financial health

criteria.name: Return on Investment
criteria.definition: Does the response weigh what a spend or effort returns against what it costs, choosing the higher-return option, rather than spending without asking what it yields?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Compares the expected return of an option against its cost, and prefers the one that pays back more.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Spends without asking what it yields; no comparison of return against cost across options.

criteria.name: Quantifying with Financial Evidence
criteria.definition: Does the response support claims with numbers, a cost, a return, a target, rather than asserting something is 'worth it' or 'affordable' with nothing behind it?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Puts real (even estimated) numbers on the decision and uses them to make the case.
criteria.weak_looks_like: All adjectives, no figures; 'it'll pay off' with no estimate; a benefit claimed without any attempt to size it.

criteria.name: Interpreting Sales and Revenue Data
criteria.definition: When sales figures are in play, does the response read the trend and its cause, rather than reacting to a single number out of context?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Reads the pattern in sales data (trend, seasonality, a cause) and lets it inform the decision.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Reacts to one number; misreads a blip as a trend; ignores what's actually driving the sales figures.
criteria.coaches: Reading sales data for the real story

criteria.name: Capital Investment Decisions
criteria.definition: When a large, long-lived purchase is at stake, does the response weigh its cost against the return it will produce over time, rather than judging it by the sticker price alone?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Evaluates a big investment by the returns it produces over its life, not just its upfront cost, and compares alternatives.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Judges a major purchase by price alone; ignores the long-run return; no comparison to the alternative use of the money.
criteria.coaches: Evaluating big investments by their long-run return

criteria.name: Sources of Financing
criteria.definition: When the plan needs funding, does the response weigh the trade-offs of borrowing versus giving up ownership versus using its own cash, rather than treating all money as the same?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Weighs the cost and trade-offs of different financing sources (debt, equity, retained earnings) for this situation.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats all sources of money as interchangeable; ignores the cost or strings attached to how it's raised.
criteria.coaches: Weighing how to finance a plan

criteria.name: Comparing Options by Profitability
criteria.definition: When choosing between options, does the response compare which one actually makes more money, accounting for both revenue and cost, rather than picking on gut or revenue alone?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Compares options on the profit each would produce, weighing both the money in and the money out.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Compares on revenue or gut feel alone; picks the option that sounds bigger without checking which is more profitable.

criteria.name: Managing Financial Risk
criteria.definition: Does the response recognize where money could be lost, a bad debt, an overcommitment, a bet that fails, and guard against it, rather than assuming the finances will work out?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies a realistic financial risk and takes a concrete step to limit or hedge it.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes the finances work out; overcommits with no cushion; ignores a clear way money could be lost.

criteria.name: Managing Credit and Collections
criteria.definition: When the business extends credit or waits to be paid, does the response manage the risk of not being paid, rather than assuming every customer pays on time?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes the risk in extending credit and manages it (terms, limits, collection), balancing sales against getting paid.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Extends credit freely with no thought to collection; assumes everyone pays; ignores the cost of money tied up in receivables.
criteria.coaches: Managing the risk of extending credit

criteria.name: Forecasting and Projections
criteria.definition: When the plan depends on the future, does the response make a reasoned estimate of what's likely, grounded in something, rather than assuming best-case or guessing blindly?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Grounds a forward estimate in evidence or a stated assumption, and acknowledges it could be off.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes best-case; projects with no basis; treats an optimistic guess as a certainty.

criteria.name: Setting Financial Goals and Targets
criteria.definition: Does the response set concrete financial targets to aim at and measure against, rather than pursuing 'more money' with no number?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Sets a specific financial target (a revenue, margin, or cost number) that gives the plan a measurable aim.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Vague 'increase profit' with no target; no number to steer by or measure against.

criteria.name: Financial Record-Keeping
criteria.definition: Does the response value keeping accurate financial records, so decisions rest on real numbers, rather than treating bookkeeping as optional?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes that accurate records underpin good decisions and treats keeping them as essential, not busywork.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Dismisses record-keeping; relies on rough guesses; makes decisions with no reliable financial data behind them.

criteria.name: Workforce Planning
criteria.definition: Does the response think about what roles and how many people the work actually needs, rather than staffing by habit or guessing?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Matches staffing to the actual demands of the work, anticipating where more or fewer people are needed.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Staffs by habit or gut; over- or under-staffs with no reasoning tied to the work.

criteria.name: Job Design and Roles
criteria.definition: Does the response define roles and responsibilities clearly, who owns what, rather than leaving duties vague or overlapping?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Defines clear roles and responsibilities so people know what they own and duties don't fall through the cracks.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Vague or overlapping roles; no clarity on who owns what; duties left ambiguous.

criteria.name: Recruiting and Selecting People
criteria.definition: Does the response think about getting the right person into the right role, what the role needs and how to find and choose for it, rather than filling a seat?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Defines what the role truly requires and chooses a way to find and evaluate candidates against that.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Hires generically or for the wrong traits; treats any candidate as interchangeable.
criteria.coaches: Matching the right people to roles

criteria.name: Onboarding and Setting Up for Success
criteria.definition: Does the response set new people up to succeed, orientation, expectations, support, rather than expecting them to figure it out alone?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Gives a new person the context, expectations, and support they need to become effective quickly.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Throws people in with no orientation; assumes they'll figure it out; sets no early expectations.
criteria.coaches: Setting new people up to succeed

criteria.name: Training and Developing People
criteria.definition: Does the response invest in building people's skills, rather than expecting performance without preparing anyone for it?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Identifies a specific skill gap and a concrete way to close it, tying development to better performance.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes people already know how; blames performance without building capability.

criteria.name: Supervising and Managing Others
criteria.definition: Does the response manage people day to day in a way that keeps them productive and supported, direction plus support, rather than either abandoning or micromanaging them?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Gives people clear direction and the right level of support, adjusting to what each person needs to perform.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Micromanages or abandons; one rigid style for everyone; leaves people unsure what's expected or unsupported.

criteria.name: Performance Management
criteria.definition: Does the response set clear expectations and hold people to them fairly, with feedback and consequences, rather than leaving performance undefined?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Sets a clear expectation, gives honest feedback against it, and follows through fairly.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Vague expectations; avoids hard feedback; ignores a performance problem or handles it unfairly.
criteria.coaches: Setting expectations and holding people accountable

criteria.name: Coaching and Feedback
criteria.definition: Does the response help people improve through specific, constructive feedback, rather than only criticizing, or saying nothing until it's too late?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Gives timely, specific, constructive feedback aimed at helping the person get better.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Only criticizes, or stays silent until a problem is severe; feedback is vague or purely negative.

criteria.name: Handling Underperformance
criteria.definition: When someone isn't meeting the bar, does the response address it directly and fairly, a real path to improve or a fair exit, rather than ignoring it or acting harshly?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Addresses underperformance directly with a fair, concrete path to improve, and follows through consistently.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores the problem and lets it fester, or reacts harshly with no fair chance to improve.

criteria.name: Designing Motivating Work
criteria.definition: Does the response think about what makes work motivating, challenge, purpose, autonomy, reward, rather than assuming people are driven by pay alone or by orders?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Shapes the work or its rewards around what actually motivates people, not just pay or command.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes money or orders are the only levers; ignores what would make the work engaging.

criteria.name: Compensation and Recognition
criteria.definition: Does the response use pay, rewards, and recognition to motivate fairly, rather than assuming money alone works, or ignoring recognition entirely?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Uses a fair mix of pay, incentives, and recognition matched to what actually motivates the people involved.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Assumes money is the only lever, or ignores recognition; rewards that wouldn't actually motivate.
criteria.coaches: Motivating with fair pay and recognition

criteria.name: Team Culture and Engagement
criteria.definition: Does the response build an environment people want to work in, fairness, morale, purpose, rather than treating culture as irrelevant to results?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Connects morale, fairness, or purpose to results and proposes something concrete to strengthen the environment.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores morale and culture; assumes people will perform regardless of the environment.

criteria.name: Diversity and Inclusion at Work
criteria.definition: Does the response build a workplace where different people are treated fairly and can contribute, rather than a one-mold culture that excludes?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes the value of a diverse workforce and takes concrete steps so all employees are treated fairly and included.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores fairness and inclusion; tolerates bias; a culture that would exclude or alienate people who differ.

criteria.name: Employee Well-being
criteria.definition: Does the response consider employees' well-being and sustainable workload, rather than driving people in a way that burns them out?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Attends to employees' well-being and a sustainable pace, recognizing that burnout costs the business too.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores workload and well-being; drives people to burnout; treats employees as machines to run at full tilt.

criteria.name: Retention and Turnover
criteria.definition: Does the response think about keeping good people and the cost of losing them, rather than treating employees as easily replaceable?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Recognizes the cost of turnover and proposes a concrete reason good people would stay.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Treats people as disposable; ignores turnover; assumes replacements are free and instant.

criteria.name: Succession and Talent Pipeline
criteria.definition: Does the response plan for the future need for talent, developing people for bigger roles, avoiding gaps, rather than only staffing for today?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Anticipates future talent needs and develops people or a pipeline so key roles won't be left unfilled.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Staffs only for the present; no plan for who steps up when a key person leaves.
criteria.coaches: Building a pipeline of future talent

criteria.name: Fair and Legal Treatment
criteria.definition: Does the response treat employees fairly and within the law, no discrimination, safe conditions, due process, rather than acting as if the employer had no obligations?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Keeps people-decisions fair and lawful, recognizing the employee's rights and the employer's duties.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Proposes unfair, unsafe, or unlawful treatment; ignores employees' rights entirely.

criteria.name: Employee Voice and Relations
criteria.definition: Does the response give employees a way to raise concerns and be heard, and take it seriously, rather than ignoring grievances until they blow up?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Creates a real channel for employees to raise concerns and responds to them, heading off resentment and turnover.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Ignores or suppresses employee concerns; no channel to be heard; lets grievances build with no response.

criteria.name: Customer-Centered Thinking
criteria.definition: Does the response start from the customer and work back to the offer, rather than starting from what the business wants to sell and hoping customers want it?
criteria.strong_looks_like: Anchors decisions in what the customer wants and shapes the offer to fit, not the other way around.
criteria.weak_looks_like: Starts from the product and assumes demand; the customer is an afterthought, not the starting point.
